items.title: Dan Wall and Adam Nussbaum interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 19, 2001
items.q: And like when I first heard Thelonious Monk live I could not believe how much sound he got out of the piano without banging.

ctx.x: That gets their attention. But you’ve got to be there. I mean there’s nothing like being on the bandstand playing with it. But to be in the room, to be a drummer and to watch how this motion makes the sound. To feel what’s going on. To see how the horn player plays. To watch their whole physical being and to feel the sound. I mean I was deceived for many years when I used to listen to records, because whenever I used to hear Stan Getz on a record he had that soft, gentle tone. And then I would hear Joe Henderson…

ability of his sound to project was like getting hit with a hammer wrapped in velvet. I mean he was so loud. It was deceptive. You’d never get that from a record. You’d never get it. And like when I first heard Thelonious Monk live I could not believe how much sound he got out of the piano without banging. It was like there was mac trucks behind each finger putting out the sound. Astounding.

Yeah I remember that too, the first time I heard Monk at the Vanguard. Because that’s a good example of drawing a sound out of the instrument. It’s not done with force and attack and this and that. He was pulling the sound out. Or hearing Elvin live the first time.
